text: Anthropic spent nearly $10 billion on compute and infrastructure in the third quarter of 2026, or close to $40 billion on an annualized basis, up from just $433 million in 2023. By comparison, OpenAI appears to have roughly tripled its compute spending annually and forecasts similar growth for 2026, though data for OpenAI is sparser. Most of Anthropic and OpenAI’s compute spending goes to cloud partners such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and SpaceX, which rent compute capacity to Anthropic and OpenAI. Much of Anthropic’s compute spend growth this year is attributable to SpaceX: Anthropic paid SpaceX around $5 billion for compute in the third quarter of 2026, roughly half of Anthropic’s total compute spending that quarter. We compile reports and disclosures about Anthropic and OpenAI’s spending on compute over time, and convert these figures into spending run rates to estimate how quickly each company has ramped up their compute spending over the past several years. For Anthropic, we use compute spending figures from the company’s Form S-1 , filed in advance of its IPO. The S-1 disclosed “compute and infrastructure” spending for the seven calendar quarters from 2025 through Q3 2026, as well as annual totals in 2023 and 2024 . It also disclosed spending commitments of $447.5 billion, “substantially all” related to compute and infrastructure, from September 2026 through the end of 2030, or around $100 billion per year. We primarily rely on the amended S-1 filed on November 2; the original is also available. For OpenAI, we source compute spend from media reports. The figures are compiled in our AI companies data explorer, along with earlier reports about Anthropic. However, as of this writing, the explorer only visualizes annual totals through 2025, and does not include quarterly spending disclosures from Anthropic’s S-1. Additionally, OpenAI President Greg Brockman testified in May 2026 that the company expects to spend $50 billion on compute this year, but we do not have any non-forecasted figures for OpenAI in 2026. Because these spending figures are a mix of quarterly and annual data, they need to be converted to annualized run rates for direct comparison. This requires some estimation and interpolation, which is explained below. We do not adjust for inflation. Code for the data analysis can be found in this notebook . All of Anthropic and OpenAI’s compute spend figures are period-based totals for a given year or quarter. To compare a mix of annual and quarterly data, we convert them into estimated annualized spending rates. For quarterly numbers, this means multiplying the spending amount by four. We also need to attribute the spending rates for each period to an exact date. We assign each spending estimate a date by assuming that spending grew at a steady exponential rate between reporting periods. The dates are one to three days after the midpoint of the quarter, or two to four weeks after the midpoint of the year. We then fit growth rates to these points via a log-linear regression. We derive 90% confidence intervals analytically using standard errors. Uncertainty in the assigned dates introduces an additional source of uncertainty, but modeling it had little effect on the resulting confidence intervals. Both Anthropic and OpenAI rely primarily on compute capacity from cloud partners such as Amazon, CoreWeave, Google, Microsoft, Oracle, and SpaceX. It would be misleading to compare upfront compute spending (e.g. capital expenditures) with ongoing operating expenses on cloud compute, but neither company incurs a significant amount of upfront compute spending. Per its S-1, Anthropic will increasingly use TPUs that it leases directly (“Anthropic Direct”), but these lease payments will still be amortized (discussed further in previous commentary ). Most of Anthropic’s compute is used internally for R&D and other purposes, not to serve external customers. Anthropic’s S-1 discloses its customer inference spending as “cost of revenue,” which is “substantially all” compute: “Cost of revenue” is a slight underestimate of external inference spending because Anthropic classifies compute used by free-tier customers as sales and marketing expenses rather than cost of revenue. Anthropic’s sales and marketing expenses in the first nine months of 2026 were $5.5 billion, and most of the year-on-year growth in these expenses—$4.8 billion out of a total $5.2 billion increase—came from revenue-sharing fees paid to cloud partners, not compute costs. This means that total free-tier compute spend is minor, at most in the hundreds of millions. By comparison, media reports indicate that around 50% of OpenAI’s compute spending was allocated to customer inference in 2025, up from roughly one-third in 2024. We do not have full data on each developer’s spending with its cloud partners, but Anthropic made up 34.5% of SpaceX’s total revenue in Q3 2026, or around $5 billion, half of Anthropic’s compute spend that quarter. In terms of future growth, Anthropic has also already contractually committed to $447.5 billion in future compute spending through 2030 per its S-1. This would be roughly another doubling from the current rate, so it is not clear that Anthropic’s future compute spending will grow at anywhere near the 4x annual growth of the past three years, though the company notes that it may spend even more on compute before 2030 than this current committed total. Meanwhile, OpenAI plans to spend around $750 billion on compute over the same period. AI company data, with data on revenue, funding, staff, and compute for many of the key players in frontier AI.
